clue.text: Almost lose sight of mischievous spirit

indicators.note: What is almost there falls just short, so the last letter of the phrase is dropped.

parts.note: Losing your sight is a two-word phrase, a verb of becoming plus sightless; its first word, the verb, is used whole.
The second word of that phrase, with its last letter cut off.

explanation.surface: Someone is bewitched by an impish sprite until they can barely see.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase GO BLIND is what "lose sight" gives, and "Almost" trims only its final D.
explanation.definitionFit: A goblin is a small, mischievous creature of folklore.

clue.text: It may well be read below stairs

definitions.text: It may well be read below stairs

parts.note: the surface wants a book or letter; what is read here is a dial showing units used
the surface wants the servants' quarters; here it is the cupboard under the stairs, where British homes often keep the supply

explanation.surface: A book or letter is being read in the servants' quarters of a grand house.
explanation.walkthrough: "Below stairs" suggests servants reading, but meters are "read" by the gas company, and they are often kept under the stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas meter is read to record usage and commonly sits in the cupboard under the stairs in British homes.

clue.text: Like the toast that's mostly spoken

definitions.text: Like the toast that's mostly spoken

parts.note: toast here is bread, not a speech: it describes how the slice is spread
all but the first letter of the answer is a word for spoken

explanation.surface: An after-dinner toast is mostly talk rather than drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Toast here is bread, not a speech; the joke is that BUTTERED, all but its first letter, is UTTERED, meaning spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Buttered describes toast spread with butter, the usual way it is eaten.

clue.text: Matter brought up in arithmetic

indicators.note: In a down entry, what is brought up is read from the bottom upwards, so the letters run in reverse.
The answer sits in the next word, inside its run of letters.

parts.note: Four letters sitting inside ariTHMETIc: M, E, T, I.

explanation.surface: A topic has been raised during a maths lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: "Brought up" looks like "raised for discussion", which suits "Matter", but in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a matter or point on a list or agenda.

clue.text: Pre-war competition?

parts.note: the period of military build-up that precedes fighting
a contest between nations to out-arm each other, not a sporting event

explanation.surface: A sporting contest held in the years before a war.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: the competition is between nations stockpiling weapons, which often comes before war.
explanation.definitionFit: An arms race is a contest between countries to build up weapons.

clue.text: Record of ex-officers, the retiring sort, it seems

definitions.meaning: the naval register of retired officers liable to recall
read literally: a list of the reserved, that is, the shy

explanation.surface: A register of former officers turns out to be full of shy types.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the phrase literally: a list of the reserved, that is, the retiring or shy.
explanation.definitionFit: The reserved list is the register of retired naval officers who can be recalled.

clue.text: Such a night leads to serious trouble — and gaol!

indicators.note: The leads of words are their first letters, taken from the words that follow.

parts.note: First letters of Serious, Trouble, And, Gaol.

explanation.surface: A wild night out ends with arrests and a spell in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag night is the British name for a groom's party before his wedding, notorious for ending in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Stag is the British adjective for an all-male party before a wedding, so "such a night" is a stag night.

clue.text: Sharp spies about to ensnare detectives

indicators.note: About means turned round, so the spies' letters are written backwards.
What ensnares something traps it inside, so the detectives go within.

parts.note: The CIA is the US spy agency.
CID, the Criminal Investigation Department, is the British police detective branch.

explanation.surface: Some sharp-witted agents circle round to trap police detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: "Sharp" looks like it describes the spies, but it is the definition, standing apart at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of taste: acids taste sour, so something acidic is sharp.

clue.text: Being like a bird in east New York

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east.

indicators.note: The bird goes in, placed inside the letters for New York.

parts.note: NY is the standard abbreviation for New York.
The tit is a small garden bird.

explanation.surface: Someone feels like a bird trapped in the eastern side of New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the noun: a being, not the verb "being".
explanation.definitionFit: An entity is a being, something that exists in its own right.

clue.text: Man's best friend, maybe, created this!

definitions.meaning: a dog, here a gundog breed
the person who made this crossword

explanation.surface: A dog lover boasts that the family pet invented something.
explanation.walkthrough: "This" is the crossword itself, and the person who creates one is its setter; the other setter is a gundog.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter is a breed of dog, and a crossword's author is its setter.

clue.text: Attempt is first of thousands for Montaigne, say

parts.note: To essay is to attempt; an essay is also an attempt.
Used as it stands.

indicators.note: Only the first letter of the next word is taken.

parts.note: First letter of thousands.

explanation.surface: A remark that Montaigne began by writing thousands of trial pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: Montaigne, the 16th-century French writer, invented the essay form; "say" marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Montaigne founded the essay as a form.

clue.text: Shine, bilingually

parts.note: a glossy finish for wood
two languages named side by side, one from France and one from Poland

explanation.surface: A word for gleam, given in two languages.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bilingually" hints at two languages, French and Polish, which together name the high-gloss wood finish.
explanation.definitionFit: French polish is a shellac finish that gives furniture a deep shine.

clue.text: Garden shed enthusiasts have the prototype

indicators.note: The words have the answer, holding it within their letters.

parts.note: Inside shED ENthusiasts.

explanation.surface: Hobbyists who love garden sheds own the original model.
explanation.walkthrough: Eden is the prototype garden, the first one in Genesis, so "the prototype" sharpens the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eden was the first garden, the model for all others.

clue.text: Faithful argue endlessly in cathedral city

indicators.note: Without their ends, so the last letter of each word goes.

parts.note: TRUE with its last letter cut.
ROW, to argue, with its last letter cut.

explanation.surface: Loyal churchgoers keep squabbling in a cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: "Endlessly" applies to both words. Row, rhyming with cow, is a British word for a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Truro, in Cornwall, has a Victorian cathedral and city status.

clue.text: Colour can, with time

parts.note: A tin is a can.
T is the abbreviation for time.

explanation.surface: An instruction that a can of paint will change colour over time.
explanation.walkthrough: "Colour" is the definition, not a verb acting on "can".
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tint is a shade or hue.

clue.text: Men in food riot are united

indicators.note: A riot is disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order.

parts.note: The letters to rearrange.

explanation.surface: Hungry men rioting over food show solidarity.
explanation.walkthrough: "In" looks like a placement word but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: people who share an opinion are said to be of one mind.

clue.text: Girl donating heart and liver, for example

indicators.note: Giving away her heart, the word loses its middle letters.

parts.note: GIRL with its heart, IR, removed.
Used as it stands.

explanation.surface: A young woman is an organ donor, giving her heart and her liver.
explanation.walkthrough: The organ-donation surface makes "heart" and "liver" look like a pair; only the liver is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the liver secretes bile, which makes it a gland.

clue.text: Easy passage for a camel, apparently

definitions.text: Easy passage for a camel, apparently

parts.note: the surface pictures a smooth desert route; the setter means a tiny opening
points to the Gospel saying that a camel passes through it more easily than a rich man enters heaven

explanation.surface: A route that a camel finds simple to travel.
explanation.walkthrough: Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter heaven; "apparently" nods to that saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverbial image from the Gospels, where the tiny needle opening is paradoxically easier for a camel than heaven for the rich.

clue.text: Black Prince turns out smarter

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils.
Prince Rainier III ruled Monaco.

explanation.surface: The Black Prince, Edward III's son, proves to be the cleverer one.
explanation.walkthrough: "Black Prince" reads as Edward of Woodstock, but it splits into B and a different prince, Rainier of Monaco.
explanation.definitionFit: Brainier means more intelligent, that is smarter.

clue.text: Blotches skins develop, injecting drug

indicators.note: To develop is to change form, so the letters are rearranged.
Injecting puts one thing inside another, so the drug goes within.

parts.note: The letters of SKINS rearranged.
Pot is slang for cannabis.

explanation.surface: Skin blemishes appear after someone injects a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes "Blotches" look like skin marks, but they are ink stains.
explanation.definitionFit: Blots of spilt ink are called inkspots, the stains the definition names.

clue.text: Where steeplechasers go, sooner or later

definitions.meaning: the long race over fences they are running

explanation.surface: Steeplechase runners will get where they are going eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: A steeplechase is a long race over obstacles, so its runners are literally in the long run.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning eventually, and literally the long race steeplechasers run.

clue.text: Authorise advice for hair treatment

definitions.meaning: split in two, it is an instruction to give the hair a perm

explanation.surface: A salon needs official approval before giving advice on hair.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer: PERM IT is the advice to give the hair a perm.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym, allow, while the split reading gives an instruction to a hairdresser.

clue.text: Jump like a big cat, under pressure

indicators.note: In a down entry, what is under comes lower down.

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for pressure.
The ounce is another name for the snow leopard.

explanation.surface: A big cat leaps when it is under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: The ounce is a lesser-known name for the snow leopard, and it also looks like a weight, not a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: To pounce is to jump suddenly, as a cat does on prey.

clue.text: Oral taken in college

indicators.note: Oral means by mouth, so what follows is heard rather than read.

parts.note: Food taken in has been swallowed; that past participle, spoken, fits the letters wanted.

explanation.surface: A spoken exam is sat at a college.
explanation.walkthrough: "Oral" looks like a noun for an exam, but it is the signal word; "taken in" means swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is the famous English public school.

clue.text: Does highest in pecking order rule it?

definitions.text: Does highest in pecking order rule it?

parts.note: the cockerel, top of the farmyard hierarchy
the idiom for being in charge names the place hens perch

explanation.surface: A question about whether the top ranked in a hierarchy is in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The top of the pecking order among hens is the rooster, who proverbially rules the roost.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is where birds settle, and to rule the roost is to be in charge.

clue.text: What some doctors do in return for little drinks

indicators.note: In return means going back, so the word is written backwards.

parts.note: Spin doctors spin: they put a favourable slant on news.

explanation.surface: Doctors accept small drinks as payment.
explanation.walkthrough: "Doctors" suggests medicine, but spin doctors are political press officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A nip is a small drink of spirits.

clue.text: See 15
Pocket item, one with rotating ball, appropriately

indicators.note: Rotating turns the ball round, so its letters run backwards.
The one is held with the ball, inside it.

parts.note: An orb is a ball.
I is the Roman numeral one.

explanation.surface: A pen in the pocket has a turning ball at its tip.
explanation.walkthrough: A Biro, British for a ballpoint pen, works by a rotating ball, which is why the wordplay is "appropriate".
explanation.definitionFit: A Biro is a ballpoint pen, commonly carried in a pocket.

clue.text: Little chap reportedly mad to joinin

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the answer is what the phrase is heard as.

parts.note: Mad gives an adjective for frenzied, which is joined to IN and the pair spoken as one word.

explanation.surface: A small man is said to be crazy to join in.
explanation.walkthrough: The scraped clue runs "join in" together; the wordplay is MANIC joined to IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A diminutive: the -kin suffix means small, so a mannikin is a tiny man.

clue.text: After fifty I offer love … and lust!

indicators.note: The rest is placed after the fifty.

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty.
Used as it stands.
A bid is an offer.
Love is zero in tennis, O.

explanation.surface: Someone past fifty offers love and admits to lust.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fifty" reads as an age, which is the joke of the surface; it is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: libido is sexual drive.

clue.text: A brother's dated plays appear on stage

indicators.note: Letters that play move about freely, so they are rearranged.

parts.note: The letters to rearrange.

explanation.surface: A sibling's old-fashioned plays are finally staged.
explanation.walkthrough: "Plays" looks like the theatre noun that suits the surface, but it is the verb telling the letters to move.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre idiom: the boards are the stage floor, so treading them means acting.
